title: BEFORE TIMOTHY EVER PREACHED THE GOSPEL, TWO WOMEN PREACHED IT WITH THEIR LIVES.
paragraphs: BEFORE TIMOTHY EVER PREACHED THE GOSPEL, TWO WOMEN PREACHED IT WITH THEIR LIVES.
Paul remembered their names. Heaven knew their sacrifices. And the sincere faith of a grandmother and a mother became part of a legacy that would outlive them both.
Never underestimate what God can do through a praying grandmother, a faithful mother, and a child who grows up watching them trust Jesus.
You may never stand behind a pulpit.

You may never preach before thousands of people. Your name may never appear in a Christian history book. You may spend most of your life washing dishes, working exhausting shifts, preparing meals, wiping away tears, and whispering prayers when everyone else is asleep.
You may even wonder whether anything you are doing matters.
But what if one of the greatest contributions you will ever make to the Kingdom of God is someone you are raising right now?
Someone whose little hands you once held.
Someone whose salvation you have been praying for.
Someone who may have forgotten your words but will someday remember your faith.

There is a remarkably beautiful moment in Scripture when the apostle Paul, writing to his beloved spiritual son Timothy, remembers two women whose names could easily have been overlooked by the world.
Lois and Eunice.
A grandmother.
A mother.
Two women whose sincere faith was important enough to be recorded in the eternal Word of God.
Paul writes in 2 Timothy 1:5 (KJV):
Read that again.
Before Paul speaks about Timothy stirring up his spiritual gift, before reminding him not to be ashamed of the testimony of Christ, he remembers the faith that lived in the generations before him.
In the original Greek, Paul describes Timothy's faith as:
ἀνυποκρίτου πίστεως — anypokritou pisteōs
Literally, faith without hypocrisy. Genuine faith. Sincere faith. Faith without pretense.
Not a religious performance.
Not a carefully manufactured image of holiness.
Not the kind of Christianity that looks beautiful in public but becomes unrecognizable behind closed doors.
Paul also uses the Greek word ἐνῴκησεν — enōkēsen, meaning dwelt or lived within.
The faith Paul remembered was not merely something Lois and Eunice professed. It was something that dwelt within them.
And there is an enormous difference between having Christianity displayed in your house and having Christ reigning in your heart.
You can have a Bible on every table and still refuse to forgive.
You can have Scripture written on your walls while bitterness lives within your family.
You can teach your children worship songs while showing them nothing but anger, pride, dishonesty, and condemnation.
You can take them to church every Sunday and unintentionally teach them to associate Christianity with hypocrisy throughout the rest of the week.
Children may forget the sermons they hear.
But they often remember the Christianity they experience at home.

They remember how you treated people who disappointed you. They remember whether you apologized when you were wrong. They remember what happened when money became scarce, when sickness entered the family, when someone betrayed you, and when life refused to go according to your plans.
They are watching what your faith becomes when your circumstances stop cooperating.
And perhaps that is one of the most powerful things about Paul's description of Lois and Eunice.
He did not call their faith impressive.
He called it sincere.

Scripture does not tell us every detail of their lives. We do not know how many sleepless nights they experienced, what struggles they endured, or how often they felt inadequate. We must be careful not to invent their stories simply to make them more dramatic.
But Scripture gives us something extraordinary.
Acts 16:1 identifies Timothy as the son of a believing Jewish woman and a Greek father. Later, in 2 Timothy 3:14–15, Paul reminds Timothy that he had known the sacred Scriptures from childhood.
The Greek expression used there is ἀπὸ βρέφους — apo brephous, meaning from infancy or from earliest childhood.
Long before Timothy became Paul's ministry companion, long before he was entrusted with responsibilities within the early Church, the sacred Scriptures were already part of his life.
Taken together, these passages strongly suggest the profound spiritual influence of his mother and grandmother.
Someone helped lay the foundation.
Someone made the Scriptures familiar to him.
Someone lived a faith worth remembering.
And although Paul never suggests that Timothy inherited salvation through his family, he recognizes the genuine faith that existed in the generations before him.
That distinction matters.
Faith can be modeled, taught, encouraged, and nurtured, but salvation cannot be inherited.
John 1:12–13 teaches that becoming a child of God is not ultimately a matter of human ancestry. Ephesians 2:8–9 reminds us that salvation is by grace through faith, not through our works.
Lois could not repent on Timothy's behalf.
Eunice could not believe on Timothy's behalf.
Their faithfulness could point him toward the truth, but only Jesus Christ could save him.
And that is where this story becomes deeply personal.
Because perhaps you are reading this with a broken heart.
You raised your children in church, but they no longer want anything to do with God.
You taught them to pray, but now they refuse to pray.
You remember holding their hands when they were little, and today you struggle even to have a conversation with them.
You have watched someone you love walk toward choices you begged them not to make.
And somewhere in the silence, you began asking yourself a question that has been quietly destroying you.
Where did I go wrong?
There may be things you genuinely need to acknowledge, confess, and change. There may be wounds that require an apology rather than another sermon.
But another person's unbelief is not automatically proof that you failed as a parent.
You are responsible for your faithfulness.
You are not sovereign over another person's heart.
Even the most faithful Christian parent cannot manufacture repentance, force genuine conversion, or guarantee another person's spiritual future.
Paul himself understood the limits of human ministry when he wrote in 1 Corinthians 3:6:
“I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase.”
Plant.
Water.
Pray.
Love.
Speak the truth.
Repent when necessary.
And remember who gives the increase.
God.
Perhaps you have been trying to carry a responsibility that belongs to Him alone.
Perhaps your prayers have become desperate because you cannot see any evidence that the seeds you planted are growing.
But an absence of visible results does not mean that your obedience was meaningless.
Do not confuse what you cannot see with what God cannot do.
Keep praying without attempting to control. Keep loving without compromising biblical truth. Keep the door open for reconciliation wherever it is safe and possible.
And when your heart becomes exhausted, remember that the Savior you are asking your children to trust is also the Savior inviting you to rest in Him.

Not because typing those words will guarantee someone's salvation, but because there are other mothers, fathers, grandparents, and wounded believers who need to know they are not carrying these burdens alone.
And perhaps your story is different.
Perhaps you never had a Lois.
Perhaps you never had a Eunice.
Perhaps your grandmother never prayed with you. Your mother never opened a Bible. Your father never showed you what a godly man looked like.
Perhaps the people who were supposed to introduce you to love became the very people who taught you to fear it.
Maybe your childhood was filled with abandonment, addiction, violence, betrayal, or religious hypocrisy.
Maybe the word family brings more pain than comfort.
Listen carefully.
The absence of a godly legacy does not disqualify you from beginning one.
You do not need a perfect spiritual ancestry to become a new creation in Jesus Christ.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”
The Greek expression καινὴ κτίσις — kainē ktisis means new creation.
The Gospel is not merely about improving the person you used to be.
It is about the transforming work of God through Jesus Christ, bringing you into a new life that your past could never produce on its own.
Your family history may explain some of your wounds.
It does not have the final authority over your identity in Christ.
Through His death and resurrection, Jesus offers forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and new life to those who repent and believe in Him.
You may be the first person in your family to take the Gospel seriously.
The first to confront generations of destructive behavior.
The first to apologize to your children.
The first to reject the bitterness everyone else justified.
The first to choose biblical faithfulness over the patterns you inherited.
You may not have received a legacy like Timothy's.
But by the grace of God, you can begin building one.
And that does not mean pretending you have everything figured out.
Sincere faith is not sinless perfection.
It is not never falling.
It is not never struggling.
It is not always knowing the right words to pray.
Sincere faith refuses to make peace with hypocrisy. It brings sin into the light, acknowledges weakness, receives correction, and returns to Jesus in repentance.
Imagine what it could mean for a child to hear a parent say:
“I was wrong. Please forgive me. What I did was not pleasing to God, and I need His grace just as much as you do.”
That moment may teach them something about the Gospel that a thousand lectures never could.
Because you are showing them that Christianity is not about pretending to be righteous.
It is about our desperate need for the One who truly is.
Jesus Christ.
The crucified and risen Savior.
The One who bore our sins.
The One who calls us out of darkness.
The One whose grace does not excuse our sin but teaches us to renounce ungodliness and live differently, as Titus 2:11–12 reminds us.
This is what it means to move from scandal to grace.
Not hiding the scandal.
Not glorifying the scandal.
Not pretending the damage never happened.
But bringing our brokenness, guilt, shame, and rebellion before Jesus Christ and allowing His truth to transform how we live.
Your children do not need you to convince them that you have never needed forgiveness.
They need to see what happens when someone genuinely receives it.
They need to see a Christianity that survives disappointment.
A Christianity that produces humility instead of superiority.
A Christianity that loves truth more than reputation.
A Christianity that is recognizable when nobody is watching.
That is the kind of sincere faith Paul remembered.
And notice something else.
Paul was an apostle. Timothy became a trusted minister of the Gospel. Yet in this deeply personal letter, the names of two women were not forgotten.
Lois.
Eunice.
The Scriptures preserve their names without recording a public sermon from either of them.
Their example reminds us that spiritual influence cannot always be measured by the size of a platform.
Sometimes discipleship happens around a dinner table.
Sometimes it happens beside a hospital bed.
Sometimes it happens when a grandmother opens her Bible and a curious child sits beside her.
Sometimes it happens when an exhausted mother chooses to pray instead of surrendering to despair.
Sometimes it happens when an imperfect father humbles himself before his family and admits that he needs Jesus.
The Kingdom of God is not built upon human celebrity.
Jesus Christ is its King, and even the most ordinary acts of obedience can serve His purposes.
So, to the grandmother who thinks she is too old to make a difference…
To the mother who feels invisible…
To the father trying to rebuild what his mistakes destroyed…
To the single parent carrying responsibilities that feel unbearable…
To the believer who grew up without a godly example…
Your opportunity to live sincerely before God has not disappeared.
You do not need a microphone to make disciples.
You do not need thousands of followers to glorify Christ.
You do not need a flawless past to demonstrate the power of repentance.
Begin with the people God has placed within your reach.
Open the Scriptures.
Pray together.
Listen.
Forgive.
Teach the truth with patience.
Let your conduct become consistent with your confession.
Deuteronomy 6:6–7 describes teaching God's words throughout the ordinary rhythms of family life—when sitting at home, walking along the way, lying down, and rising up.
Biblical discipleship was never intended to be confined to a weekly religious gathering.
It belongs in the everyday places where people learn what love, truth, holiness, and grace actually look like.

Someone scrolling through your feed may be a mother silently grieving over her children. A grandmother wondering whether her prayers matter. A young adult trying to escape the destructive patterns of their family. A wounded believer searching for a reason to return to Christ.
Not simply to increase its reach, but because someone you know may need the biblical encouragement contained in these words.
Honor their influence.
Remember their prayers.
Thank God for the people who pointed you toward the Savior.
Because the work of passing down sincere faith does not end with Lois and Eunice.
Every generation needs to hear the Gospel.
Every generation needs believers who are willing to teach it faithfully, live it sincerely, and support its proclamation generously.

If these messages have helped you understand Scripture, encouraged you during difficult seasons, challenged you to repent, or drawn your attention back to Jesus, prayerfully consider helping us continue and expand this work.
Scripture affirms the importance of supporting those who labor in teaching and proclaiming the Gospel (Galatians 6:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14).
It also reminds us in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
It is not a payment for God's favor, a requirement for salvation, or a substitute for every responsibility you have toward your local church, family, and those in need.
It is an opportunity to participate in a ministry dedicated to sharing biblical truth and encouraging deeper discipleship.
If you are looking for a meaningful way to support Gospel-centered work, we would be grateful to have you alongside us.
But the heart of this invitation is not merchandise.
It is helping more people encounter biblical truth.
It is investing in work that continually points people away from human glory and toward Jesus Christ.
Generosity is not a competition.
Jesus alone deserves the glory.
Perhaps years from now, someone will remember your name the way Paul remembered Lois and Eunice.
Not because you were famous.
Not because you were wealthy.
Not because you never made mistakes.
But because, in a world filled with counterfeit faith, they saw something genuine in you.
They saw you repent.
They saw you forgive.
They saw you cling to Scripture.
They saw you return to Jesus when everything else was falling apart.
And through your imperfect but sincere witness, they were pointed toward a perfect Savior.
You may never live long enough to witness every fruit of the seeds you plant.
But you can remain faithful to the One who gives the increase.
So keep opening that Bible.
Keep praying for that child.
Keep living what you profess.
Keep returning to the cross.
And when the enemy reminds you of everything that went wrong in your family, remember that the Gospel is not limited by the failures of previous generations.
Jesus Christ is still able to redeem sinners, restore broken lives, and make all things new.
You may have inherited a history of brokenness, but through Jesus Christ, brokenness does not have to be the legacy you leave behind.
